title: FCRA Bill — Expanding State Control Over Civil Society
description: Context: The introduction of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment (FCRA) Bill, 2026, in the Lok Sabha, has ignited intense constitutional and political debates across India. About FCRA Bill — Expanding State Control Over Civil Society: Key Features of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026: Example: Section 14B allows automatic cessation of registration during pending renewals, risking operational paralysis due to administrative delays. Example: Funding interruptions can directly affect child welfare, immunization drives, healthcare services, and skill-development programs. Example: Absence of fixed approval timelines creates uncertainty for projects dependent on sustained foreign funding. Example: Thousands of mission schools, hospitals, and orphanages may face risks of excessive regulatory intervention. Example: Section 16A permits provisional vesting of assets in government authorities without prior judicial review. Key Initiatives and Pre-Existing Frameworks Major Structural Challenges in the 2026 Bill: Example: The authority can take possession of properties, alter management arrangements, and oversee asset disposal. Example: Buildings or land can be sold, with proceeds transferred to the Consolidated Fund of India. Example: Tribal rights, environmental, or human-rights organizations could face action under vague interpretations. Example: Directors and key functionaries may be held personally liable for procedural compliance failures. Example: Section 43 requires state agencies to obtain prior Central approval before initiating investigations. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, marks a major shift from regulating foreign cash flows to introducing sweeping state control over civil society assets. By granting a centralized Designated Authority the power to seize properties without prior judicial review, the Bill risks creating a chilling effect that could disrupt essential healthcare and educational networks. Discuss the key provisions of the proposed FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026. Examine its implications for NGOs and civil society. Suggest how a balance can be achieved between regulatory oversight and institutional autonomy. (15 M)

title: India’s Free Trade Agreement Paradox
description: This editorial is based on “Four challenges that demand attention in India’s FTAs” published in The Indian Express on 08/06/2026. The article brings into focus India's rapidly expanding FTA network, which is set to cover 69 countries and nearly 75% of India's exports, underscoring its growing role in trade policy. For Prelims: Free Trade Agreement (FTA), Trade Deficit, India–EU FTA, UNCTAD, China Plus One, Rules of Origin (RoO), Most-Favored-Nation (MFN), Inverted Duty Structure, EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, MSMEs, Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme, Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs), Export Promotion Councils (EPCs). For Mains: Key facts regarding FTAs and reasons behind India moving towards FTAs, Key issues associated with India's FTAs and measures needed for best utilisation of FTAs. As India aggressively expands its Free Trade Agreement (FTA) network, now covering 15 agreements with 27 countries, it faces critical structural challenges that threaten to undermine domestic manufacturing and widen trade deficits. Failure to harmonize input duties with FTA commitments risks weakening domestic value addition and industrial capacity, potentially turning FTAs into a gateway for increased imports rather than export-led growth.

description: GS Paper III – Economy (Industrial Policy; Innovation) | GS Paper III – Science & Technology Research & Development (R&D) Investment; Innovation Ecosystem; Private Sector Behaviour Indian businesses underinvest in R&D due to a combination of structural and historical factors. Limited manufacturing depth, financialisation, and historically commerce-oriented business practices have reduced incentives for innovation. As a result, India’s R&D intensity remains below the level needed to support its long-term economic and technological ambitions. Protected domestic markets, colonial-era commercial orientation, and premature financialisation have weakened manufacturing depth and innovation incentives. Global evidence shows similar trends, with firms prioritising buybacks and dividends over long-term R&D due to short-term market pressures and high discount rates.
